thread.title: The Winning and Losing Stock Picks of 2018

title: The Winning and Losing Stock Picks of 2018
text:
The Winning and Losing Stock Picks of 2018 By Jan. 4, 2019 7:16 p.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty Images Text size
Last year was a painful one for the stock market—and for my 2018 stock picks.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed out 2018 last Monday with a New Year’s Eve rally, but that didn’t prevent the blue-chip benchmark from ending the year down 5.6%, its worst annual drop since 2008. The S&P 500 fell 6.2%, and the Nasdaq Composite declined 3.9%.
Most of the damage was done during the last three months of the year, as the Dow tumbled 12%, its worst quarterly performance since 2011. It was then that a fear of overheating quickly morphed into a fear that the economy was heading for a recession . The fact that investors’ favorite stocks— Apple (AAPL) and Amazon.com (AMZN) among them—took a beating didn’t help matters. It’s fair to say that 2018 ended with the market prepared for the worst.
Which is one way to describe my 2018 stock picks—the worst. Of the 15 specific picks I made in this space, just seven outperformed the S&P 500 over the same period, and only four had a positive return overall. In all, my picks lost an average of 4.8 percentage points more than the overall market.
Sometimes it was a question of bad timing. I recommended buying Transocean (RIG) on Oct. 5 , just as optimism about oil demand peaked and concerns about supply started bubbling up. As a result, oil tumbled 35%, and Transocean’s stock price was nearly cut in half. Still, barring a recession, buying the offshore driller in the mid-single digits would likely be a good bet.
Similarly, I whiffed on Baidu (BIDU), which I recommended because Chinese internet stocks had decoupled from their U.S. counterparts. While I was correct that they would eventually start moving together again, it occurred not because of a Baidu rally, but because U.S. internet stocks tanked. Baidu dropped 27%, or 14 percentage points more than the market, since I recommended it on Sept. 7.
Others were simply bad calls. I recommended buying Dollar Tree (DLTR) before the release of its second-quarter earnings , arguing that it its Family Dollar brand would finally show the progress investors had been waiting to see. It didn’t , and the stock dropped 15% over the next week. I also predicted a turnaround for General Mills (GIS) that never came. Its stock dropped 9.4% after my March call. More From The Trader Utility Stocks Can Be Steady Performers in Times of Turmoil
Three calls stand out on the positive side of the ledger. I recommended home-improvement chain Lowe’s (LOW) in May and Starbucks (SBUX) in June, both as turnaround plays. Lowe’s got a boost after a new CEO was named and activist investor Bill Ackman of Pershing Square took a stake in the stock. It gained 8% following my recommendation, outperforming the S&P 500 by nearly 16 percentage points. I argued that Starbucks could benefit from an activist’s involvement , and while my timing wasn’t ideal—its shares continued to slide immediately after the call—they ultimately gained 15%, or 25 percentage points more than the S&P 500, after Ackman got involved.
But in a year when it was easier making money short than long, my best call was a recommendation to sell L Brands (LB) on March 3. The stock had already gotten hit hard, but Jefferies analyst Randy Konik warned there was more downside to come as consumer tastes shifted away from Victoria’s Secret’s focus on supermodels . Shares of L Brands fell 37% after recommendation to sell, 30 percentage points more than the S&P 500 over the same period.
In 2019, I’ll do my best to find more L Brands and fewer of everything else.
